why: Each pair adds +1 to a range of indices, so a difference array gives how many copies of each arr[i] land in the new array. Then 'how many elements of the new array are smaller than arr[i]' is a counting query answered by sorting the (value, copies) pairs and taking prefix sums of the copies.
hints: The new array is a multiset: what matters is how many times each index is copied into it. How can you add 1 over many ranges cheaply?
Difference array over the pairs gives cnt[i] = copies of arr[i]. Indices with cnt[i] = 0 are the ones that score; their score is the number of copies of values strictly smaller than arr[i].
Sort (value, cnt) for indices with cnt > 0, build prefix sums of cnt, and for each unused index binary-search the first value >= arr[i]. O((n + m) log n).
pitfalls: Repeated or overlapping pairs count their elements multiple times; the new array is a concatenation, not a union.
Use strictly smaller: equal values do not count (use bisect_left).
Building the concatenated array explicitly can be O(n * m) elements; count copies instead.
statement:
You are given an integer array arr of size n and m pairs [start, end] (inclusive, 0-based). Concatenate the subarrays arr[start..end] for every pair, in order, into a new array efficient (overlapping and repeated pairs copy their elements again).

For each index i of arr:

  • if index i lies in at least one pair's range, its efficiency is 0;
  • otherwise its efficiency is the number of elements of efficient whose value is strictly smaller than arr[i].

Return the sum of all efficiencies.

Worked example. arr = [1, 2, 3, 2, 4, 5], pairs = [[0,1],[3,4],[0,0],[3,4]].

  • Subarrays: [1,2], [2,4], [1], [2,4], so efficient = [1,2,2,4,1,2,4].
  • Indices 0, 1, 3, 4 are used: efficiency 0.
  • Index 2 (value 3): smaller elements are 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, so 5.
  • Index 5 (value 5): all 7 elements are smaller, so 7.
  • Total: 5 + 7 = 12.
constraints:
• Numeric bounds are not stated in the source. Reasonable: 1 <= n, m <= 10^5, 1 <= arr[i] <= 10^9
  • 0 <= pairs[j][0] <= pairs[j][1] < n
  • The answer can exceed 32 bits.
